questions.questionTextEn: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of $14$, $15$, and $21$?
questions.explanationEn: Write the prime factorizations: $14 = 2 \times 7$, $15 = 3 \times 5$, and $21 = 3 \times 7$. Taking the highest power of each prime gives $\text{LCM}(14, 15, 21) = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 210$.

questions.questionTextEn: What is the measure of each exterior angle of a regular $12$-sided polygon (regular dodecagon)?
questions.explanationEn: The sum of the exterior angles of any convex polygon is $360^\circ$. For a regular $n$-sided polygon, each exterior angle measures $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$. With $n = 12$, each exterior angle is $\frac{360^\circ}{12} = 30^\circ$.

questions.questionTextEn: If the radius of a circle is increased by $10\%$, by what percentage does its area increase?
questions.explanationEn: Area scales as the square of the radius ($A = \pi r^2$). When $r$ becomes $1.10r$, the new area is $\pi(1.10r)^2 = 1.21\pi r^2 = 1.21A$, representing a $21\%$ increase.

questions.questionTextEn: Section A has $20$ students with an average score of $70$, and Section B has $30$ students with an average score of $80$. What is the combined average score of all $50$ students?
questions.explanationEn: The combined weighted average is $\frac{20 \times 70 + 30 \times 80}{20 + 30} = \frac{1400 + 2400}{50} = \frac{3800}{50} = 76$.

questions.questionTextEn: A train of length $180\text{ m}$ is traveling at a constant speed of $72\text{ km/h}$. How many seconds does it take to completely pass a stationary signal pole?
questions.explanationEn: Convert speed from $\text{km/h}$ to $\text{m/s}$: $72 \times \frac{5}{18} = 20\text{ m/s}$. To completely pass a stationary pole, the train must travel a distance equal to its own length ($180\text{ m}$), taking $t = \frac{180}{20} = 9\text{ s}$.

questions.questionTextEn: What is the area (in square units) of the triangle whose vertices in the Cartesian plane are $A(1, 2)$, $B(5, 2)$, and $C(3, 8)$?
questions.explanationEn: Vertices $A(1, 2)$ and $B(5, 2)$ lie on the horizontal line $y = 2$, forming a base of length $5 - 1 = 4\text{ units}$. The perpendicular height from $C(3, 8)$ to $y = 2$ is $8 - 2 = 6\text{ units}$. Thus, $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 6 = 12\text{ square units}$.

questions.questionTextEn: A chord of length $16\text{ cm}$ is drawn inside a circle of radius $10\text{ cm}$. What is the perpendicular distance (in $\text{cm}$) from the center of the circle to the chord?
questions.explanationEn: The perpendicular from the center bisects the chord into two equal segments of length $\frac{16}{2} = 8\text{ cm}$. Applying the Pythagorean theorem to the resulting right triangle with hypotenuse $r = 10\text{ cm}$ gives $d = \sqrt{10^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{100 - 64} = \sqrt{36} = 6\text{ cm}$.

questions.questionTextEn: If the base radius of a right circular cylinder is doubled and its height is halved, how does its volume change?
questions.explanationEn: Original volume is $V = \pi r^2 h$. With $r' = 2r$ and $h' = \frac{h}{2}$, the new volume is $V' = \pi (2r)^2 \left(\frac{h}{2}\right) = \pi (4r^2)\left(\frac{h}{2}\right) = 2\pi r^2 h = 2V$. Doubling the volume is a $100\%$ increase.

questions.questionTextEn: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the two roots of the quadratic equation $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$, what is the value of $\alpha^3 + \beta^3$?
questions.explanationEn: From Vieta's formulas, $\alpha + \beta = 5$ and $\alpha\beta = 6$ (indeed, the roots are $2$ and $3$). Using the algebraic identity $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 = (\alpha + \beta)^3 - 3\alpha\beta(\alpha + \beta) = 5^3 - 3(6)(5) = 125 - 90 = 35$.

questions.questionTextEn: How many integer values of $x$ satisfy the inequality $|2x - 5| \le 7$?
questions.explanationEn: Rewriting $|2x - 5| \le 7$ gives $-7 \le 2x - 5 \le 7$. Adding $5$ across yields $-2 \le 2x \le 12$, and dividing by $2$ gives $-1 \le x \le 6$. The integers in $[-1, 6]$ are $\{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, a total of $6 - (-1) + 1 = 8$ integers.

questions.questionTextEn: The $(E)/(Z)$ descriptor for the alkene 1-bromo-2-chloro-1-fluoroprop-1-ene in which the bromine and chlorine atoms are on the same side of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond is:
questions.explanationEn: At C1, the two attached atoms are $\text{Br}$ ($Z = 35$) and $\text{F}$ ($Z = 9$), so $-\text{Br}$ has higher CIP priority. At C2, the two attached atoms are $\text{Cl}$ ($Z = 17$) and $\text{C}$ of $-\text{CH}_3$ ($Z = 6$), so $-\text{Cl}$ has higher priority. Since both higher-priority groups ($-\text{Br}$ and $-\text{Cl}$) lie on the same side of the double bond, the configuration is $(Z)$.

questions.questionTextEn: Cobaltocene, $[\text{Co}(\eta^5\text{-C}_5\text{H}_5)_2]$, is a $19$-electron paramagnetic sandwich complex that readily acts as a
optionsEn: strong one-electron oxidizing agent to form the $20$-electron anion $[\text{Co}(\eta^5\text{-C}_5\text{H}_5)_2]^-$
strong one-electron reducing agent to form the stable $18$-electron cobaltocenium cation $[\text{Co}(\eta^5\text{-C}_5\text{H}_5)_2]^+$
diamagnetic Lewis acid that binds $\text{CO}$ without changing electron count
questions.explanationEn: Cobaltocene has $9 + 2(5) = 19$ valence electrons, placing its $19\text{th}$ electron in a high-energy antibonding $e_{1g}^*$ orbital. Loss of this single electron is thermodynamically very favorable, generating the closed-shell $18$-electron cobaltocenium cation $[\text{CoCp}_2]^+$ (isoelectronic with ferrocene); thus cobaltocene is a widely used one-electron reductant.

questions.questionTextEn: Among the following high-spin divalent first-row transition metal ions, which ion has the LARGEST octahedral site stabilization energy (OSSE, in units of $\Delta_o$, assuming $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$)?
questions.explanationEn: Using $\text{OSSE} = |\text{CFSE}_o| - |\text{CFSE}_t|$ with $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$: for $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($d^8$), $|\text{CFSE}_o| = 1.2\Delta_o$ and $|\text{CFSE}_t| = 0.8\Delta_t = 0.356\Delta_o$, giving $\text{OSSE} = 0.844\Delta_o$. For $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($d^5$), $\text{OSSE} = 0$; for $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ($d^6$), $0.4 - 0.6(4/9) = 0.133\Delta_o$; for $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ($d^7$), $0.8 - 1.2(4/9) = 0.267\Delta_o$. Thus $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ has the largest OSSE.

questions.questionTextEn: Hexachlorocyclotriphosphazene, $(\text{NPCl}_2)_3$, is prepared in the laboratory by heating
optionsEn: $\text{PCl}_5$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ in refluxing chlorobenzene or sym-tetrachloroethane
questions.explanationEn: Refluxing phosphorus pentachloride ($\text{PCl}_5$) with ammonium chloride ($\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$) in a chlorinated solvent such as chlorobenzene or $1,1,2,2$-tetrachloroethane ($\sim 135\,^\circ\text{C}$) eliminates $\text{HCl}$ to produce cyclic chlorophosphazenes, predominantly the trimer $(\text{NPCl}_2)_3$: $3\text{PCl}_5 + 3\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} \to (\text{NPCl}_2)_3 + 12\text{HCl}$. Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: On a Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plot ($\frac{1}{v}$ versus $\frac{1}{[\text{S}]}$), reversible uncompetitive inhibition produces a set of lines (at different inhibitor concentrations) that
optionsEn: intersect at a common point on the positive $y$-axis
intersect at a common point on the negative $x$-axis
are strictly parallel to each other with the same slope
questions.explanationEn: In uncompetitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex $\text{ES}$, reducing both $v_{\max}$ and $K_M$ by the same factor $\alpha' = 1 + [\text{I}]/K_I'$. Thus, the Lineweaver-Burk equation becomes $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{K_M}{v_{\max}}\frac{1}{[\text{S}]} + \frac{\alpha'}{v_{\max}}$, which retains an identical slope $\frac{K_M}{v_{\max}}$ while shifting the $y$-intercept upward, yielding parallel lines. Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: For a dilute aqueous solution of a strong electrolyte, the concentration dependence of molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ according to Kohlrausch's empirical law is:
questions.explanationEn: Kohlrausch established that for strong electrolytes in dilute solutions, molar conductivity decreases linearly with the square root of concentration due to interionic relaxation and electrophoretic effects: $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - K\sqrt{c}$, where $\Lambda_m^\circ$ is the limiting molar conductivity.

questions.questionTextEn: For a pure substance whose liquid phase is denser than its solid phase (such as water or bismuth), the slope $dP/dT$ of the solid-liquid coexistence curve in a $P$-$T$ diagram is:
optionsEn: Infinite at the normal melting point
questions.explanationEn: By the Clapeyron equation, $\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{\Delta_{\text{fus}} H_m}{T \Delta_{\text{fus}} V_m}$. Melting is always endothermic ($\Delta_{\text{fus}} H_m > 0$). When the liquid is denser than the solid, $V_{m,\text{l}} < V_{m,\text{s}}$, so $\Delta_{\text{fus}} V_m = V_{m,\text{l}} - V_{m,\text{s}} < 0$, making the slope $dP/dT$ negative.

questions.questionTextEn: The broadband proton-decoupled $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum of *para*-xylene ($1,4$-dimethylbenzene) exhibits how many distinct signals?
questions.explanationEn: *para*-Xylene ($D_{2h}$ symmetry) has $8$ carbon atoms grouped into $3$ symmetry-equivalent sets: (1) the two equivalent methyl carbons ($-\text{CH}_3$), (2) the two equivalent quaternary ipso aromatic carbons (C1 and C4), and (3) the four equivalent CH aromatic carbons (C2, C3, C5, and C6). Thus, it shows $3$ signals in its $^{13}\text{C}\{^1\text{H}\}$ NMR spectrum. Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The ground-state spectroscopic term symbol for a neutral carbon atom ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$) is
questions.explanationEn: For the $2p^2$ configuration, the Pauli-allowed terms are $^1S, ^1D, ^3P$. By Hund's first rule, the highest spin multiplicity ($^3P$, with $S = 1, L = 1$) lies lowest. Because the $2p$ subshell is less than half-filled, Hund's third rule selects the smallest total angular momentum $J = |L - S| = |1 - 1| = 0$, giving $^3P_0$. Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Electrophilic aromatic substitution on $1H$-indole (such as Vilsmeier-Haack formylation or Mannich reaction) takes place selectively at the
questions.explanationEn: Electrophilic attack at C-3 of indole yields a resonance-stabilized iminium intermediate that completely preserves the aromatic sextet of the fused benzene ring. In contrast, attack at C-2 requires disrupting benzene aromaticity to involve the nitrogen lone pair in delocalization, making C-3 strongly preferred.

questions.questionTextEn: In the Paterno-Büchi reaction, UV irradiation of benzophenone ($\text{Ph}_2\text{C}=\text{O}$) in the presence of 2-methylpropene ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$) gives predominantly:
questions.explanationEn: In the Paterno-Büchi $[2+2]$ photocycloaddition, the $n \to \pi^*$ triplet excited carbonyl oxygen of benzophenone attacks the less substituted alkene carbon (C1 of 2-methylpropene) to generate the MORE stable 1,4-diradical (having a tertiary alkyl radical at C2 and a tertiary benzhydryl radical). Spin inversion and ring closure then form **3,3-dimethyl-2,2-diphenyloxetane** (with the two methyl groups at C3, adjacent to the $\text{CPh}_2$ carbon, rather than adjacent to oxygen).

questions.questionTextEn: Singlet methylene ($^1:\text{CH}_2$) adds to $(Z)$-but-2-ene to give *cis*-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane exclusively, whereas triplet methylene ($^3:\text{CH}_2$) gives a mixture of *cis*- and *trans*-1,2-dimethylcyclopropanes. This difference arises because:
optionsEn: Singlet carbene reacts in a concerted stereospecific step, whereas triplet carbene reacts stepwise via a triplet 1,3-diradical that undergoes bond rotation prior to spin inversion
Triplet carbene reacts in a concerted step, whereas singlet carbene forms a zwitterionic intermediate
Singlet carbene is linear while triplet carbene is bent
Triplet carbene selectively isomerizes $(Z)$-but-2-ene to $(E)$-but-2-ene before cyclopropanation
questions.explanationEn: According to the Skell-Woodworth hypothesis, a singlet carbene has paired electrons in an $sp^2$ orbital and an empty $p$ orbital, enabling a single-step, concerted, stereospecific $[2+1]$ cheletropic addition. A triplet carbene has two unpaired parallel-spin electrons, so addition must occur stepwise via a triplet 1,3-diradical; C–C bond rotation competes with intersystem crossing (spin flip) before ring closure, leading to a mixture of *cis* and *trans* cyclopropanes.

questions.questionTextEn: In $^{57}\text{Fe}$ Mössbauer spectroscopy, the nuclear excited state ($I = 3/2$) has a smaller nuclear charge radius than the ground state ($I = 1/2$), i.e., $\Delta R / R < 0$. Consequently, as the $s$-electron density at the $^{57}\text{Fe}$ nucleus INCREASES, the Mössbauer isomer shift ($\delta$)
questions.explanationEn: The Mössbauer isomer shift is proportional to $(\Delta R / R)\left(|\psi_s(0)|^2_{\text{absorber}} - |\psi_s(0)|^2_{\text{source}}\right)$. Because $\Delta R / R < 0$ for $^{57}\text{Fe}$, increasing the $s$-electron density at the iron nucleus ($|\psi_s(0)|^2$) makes $\delta$ MORE NEGATIVE (smaller). Thus high-spin $\text{Fe(III)}$ ($3d^5$, less $d$-shielding of $3s$) has a smaller $\delta$ than high-spin $\text{Fe(II)}$ ($3d^6$).

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following octahedral complexes are DIAMAGNETIC ($S = 0$)?
questions.explanationEn: (A) $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ is low-spin $d^6$ ($t_{2g}^6$, $0$ unpaired electrons $\implies$ diamagnetic). (B) $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ is high-spin $d^6$ ($t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$, $4$ unpaired electrons $\implies$ paramagnetic). (C) $[\text{Fe}(\text{bpy})_3]^{2+}$ is low-spin $d^6$ ($t_{2g}^6$, diamagnetic). (D) $[\text{Zn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ is $d^{10}$ ($0$ unpaired electrons, diamagnetic). Hence (A), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following are recognized properties of pseudohalogens (such as cyanogen, $(\text{CN})_2$, and thiocyanogen, $(\text{SCN})_2$) and their pseudohalide anions?
optionsEn: They form sparingly soluble silver(I), mercury(I), and lead(II) salts similar to halides.
Their conjugate acids ($\text{HCN}, \text{HN}_3$) are always stronger Brønsted acids in water than $\text{HCl}$.
Cyanogen disproportionates in aqueous alkali as $(\text{CN})_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \to \text{CN}^- + \text{OCN}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, analogous to $\text{Cl}_2$.
Pseudohalide anions such as $\text{CN}^-$ and $\text{SCN}^-$ form stable coordination complexes with transition metals.
questions.explanationEn: Pseudohalides mimic halides by forming insoluble $\text{Ag}^+, \text{Hg}_2^{2+}, \text{Pb}^{2+}$ salts (A is true), undergoing base-induced disproportionation (C is true), and acting as good ligands toward transition metals (D is true). However, unlike $\text{HCl}$, hydro-pseudohalic acids such as $\text{HCN}$ ($\text{p}K_a \approx 9.2$) and $\text{HN}_3$ ($\text{p}K_a \approx 4.7$) are weak acids in water (B is false). Thus, (A), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Regarding photophysical radiative and non-radiative transitions depicted in a Jablonski diagram, the CORRECT statement(s) is(are)
optionsEn: Fluorescence is a spin-forbidden radiative transition from $T_1$ to $S_0$.
Intersystem crossing (ISC) is a non-radiative transition between states of different spin multiplicity.
Internal conversion (IC) is a non-radiative isoenergetic transition between states of the same spin multiplicity.
Phosphorescence typically has a shorter lifetime than fluorescence.
questions.explanationEn: Fluorescence is a spin-allowed $S_1 \to S_0$ radiative transition with short lifetimes ($10^{-9}\text{--}10^{-7}\text{ s}$), whereas phosphorescence is a spin-forbidden $T_1 \to S_0$ radiative transition with much longer lifetimes ($10^{-3}\text{--}10^2\text{ s}$), making (A) and (D) false. Intersystem crossing (e.g., $S_1 \leadsto T_1$) changes spin multiplicity without photon emission (B is true), and internal conversion (e.g., $S_2 \leadsto S_1$) preserves spin multiplicity without photon emission (C is true). Thus, (B) and (C) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about the Debye-Hückel limiting law (DHLL) is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: It predicts that $\gamma_\pm < 1$ for all dilute electrolyte solutions.
It treats ions as point charges moving in a continuous dielectric medium of constant permittivity.
The mean activity coefficient $\gamma_\pm$ depends on the ionic strength $I$ and the charge product $|z_+ z_-|$.
It accurately predicts $\gamma_\pm > 1$ observed in concentrated ($> 1\text{ M}$) aqueous electrolyte solutions.
questions.explanationEn: DHLL ($\log_{10}\gamma_\pm = -A|z_+ z_-|\sqrt{I}$) assumes point-charge ions in a continuum dielectric (B), depends on $I$ and $|z_+ z_-|$ (C), and always yields $\log_{10}\gamma_\pm < 0 \implies \gamma_\pm < 1$ (A). Because it neglects finite ion size and ion-solvent salting-out effects, it cannot predict $\gamma_\pm > 1$ at high concentrations (D is false).

questions.questionTextEn: For the exothermic gas-phase equilibrium $\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g})$ ($\Delta_r H^\circ < 0$), which of the following changes will increase the equilibrium mole fraction of $\text{NH}_3$?
optionsEn: Increasing the total pressure at constant temperature
Decreasing the temperature at constant pressure
Adding an inert gas at constant temperature and constant total pressure
Removing $\text{NH}_3$ continuously while maintaining constant temperature and total pressure
questions.explanationEn: Since $\Delta \nu_g = 2 - 4 = -2 < 0$, increasing total pressure at constant $T$ shifts equilibrium toward fewer gas moles, increasing $x_{\text{NH}_3}$ (A). Since $\Delta_r H^\circ < 0$, lowering $T$ increases $K_p$ and thus increases $x_{\text{NH}_3}$ (B). Adding an inert gas at constant $T$ and $P$ lowers partial pressures and shifts the reaction backward, reducing $x_{\text{NH}_3}$ (C is false). Removing $\text{NH}_3$ drives conversion forward, but lowers the instantaneous mole fraction of $\text{NH}_3$ in the vessel (D is false).

questions.questionTextEn: The number of irreducible representations in the $C_{3v}$ point group is _____ (in integer).
questions.explanationEn: The $C_{3v}$ point group (order $h = 6$) has three classes: $\{E\}$, $\{2C_3\}$, and $\{3\sigma_v\}$. By the Great Orthogonality Theorem, the number of irreducible representations equals the number of classes, namely $3$ ($A_1, A_2, E$).

questions.questionTextEn: Given that the ionization energy of the ground-state hydrogen atom is $13.6\text{ eV}$, the ionization energy of the ground-state $\text{Li}^{2+}$ ion (in $\text{eV}$, rounded off to one decimal place) is _____.
questions.explanationEn: For a one-electron hydrogen-like ion of atomic number $Z$, the ground-state ionization energy scales as $\text{IE} = Z^2 \cdot \text{IE}(\text{H})$. For $\text{Li}^{2+}$ ($Z = 3$), $\text{IE} = 3^2 \times 13.6\text{ eV} = 9 \times 13.6\text{ eV} = 122.4\text{ eV}$.

questions.questionTextEn: The total number of distinct signals observed in the broadband proton-decoupled $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum of $1,4$-dimethoxybenzene is _____ (in integer).
questions.explanationEn: $1,4$-Dimethoxybenzene has high symmetry ($D_{2h}$ on the NMR timescale due to rapid $-\text{OCH}_3$ rotation). Its $8$ carbon atoms fall into exactly $3$ symmetry-equivalent sets: (1) the two *ipso* quaternary aromatic carbons (C1, C4), (2) the four equivalent aromatic CH carbons (C2, C3, C5, C6), and (3) the two equivalent methoxy ($-\text{OCH}_3$) carbons. Thus, $3$ signals are observed.

questions.questionTextEn: Ring-closing metathesis (RCM) of diethyl 2,2-diallylmalonate ($(\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2)_2\text{C}(\text{CO}_2\text{Et})_2$) using Grubbs' second-generation catalyst yields a cycloalkene (with elimination of ethene). The number of carbon atoms in the newly formed cycloalkene ring is _____ (in integer).
questions.explanationEn: The diene chain connecting the two internal alkene carbons is $-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ (C1–C2) linked via $-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{CO}_2\text{Et})_2-\text{CH}_2-$ to $-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. Upon extrusion of the two terminal $=\text{CH}_2$ carbons as ethene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$), the remaining $5$ carbons ($\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}-\text{CH}_2$) form diethyl cyclopent-3-ene-1,1-dicarboxylate, a $5$-membered ring.

questions.questionTextEn: For the alkaline hydrolysis of methyl benzoates in aqueous ethanol, the Hammett reaction constant is $\rho = +2.20$. Given that $\sigma_p(\text{NO}_2) = +0.78$, the ratio of rate constants $k_{p\text{-NO}_2} / k_{\text{H}}$ is _____ (rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanationEn: Using the Hammett equation $\log_{10}(k_X / k_H) = \rho \sigma_X$, we have $\log_{10}(k_{p\text{-NO}_2} / k_H) = (+2.20)(+0.78) = 1.716$. Taking the antilogarithm yields $k_{p\text{-NO}_2} / k_H = 10^{1.716} = 52.00 \approx 52.0$.

questions.questionTextEn: A radionuclide has a first-order decay constant $\lambda = 0.03465\text{ min}^{-1}$. Its half-life $t_{1/2}$ (in $\text{min}$, rounded off to one decimal place) is _______.
questions.explanationEn: For first-order radioactive decay, $t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \frac{0.69315}{0.03465\text{ min}^{-1}} = 20.004 \approx 20.0\text{ min}$.

questions.questionTextEn: Determine the ground-state effective magnetic moment (in Bohr magnetons, rounded to two decimal places) for the eight-coordinate aqua ion $[\text{Gd}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_8]^{3+}$ ($Z_{\text{Gd}} = 64$): _______.
questions.explanationEn: $\text{Gd}^{3+}$ has the half-filled $[\text{Xe}]4f^7$ configuration, giving $S = \frac{7}{2}$, $L = 0$, and $J = \frac{7}{2}$ ($^8S_{7/2}$). The Landé factor is $g_J = 2$, so $\mu = g_J\sqrt{J(J+1)} = 2\sqrt{\frac{7}{2} \times \frac{9}{2}} = \sqrt{63} = 7.9373 \approx 7.94\text{ BM}$.

questions.questionTextEn: The $(R_a)/(S_a)$ configuration of the chiral biphenyl 6,6'-dinitro-[1,1'-biphenyl]-2,2'-dicarboxylic acid, oriented with the front ring lying vertically (bearing $-\text{NO}_2$ at UP and $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ at DOWN) and the rear ring lying horizontally (bearing $-\text{NO}_2$ at LEFT and $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ at RIGHT), is:
questions.explanationEn: Assigning CIP priorities along the chiral axis (front ring first, then rear ring): on each ring, $-\text{NO}_2$ ($\text{N}$, $Z=7$) has higher priority than $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ ($\text{C}$, $Z=6$). Thus: front $-\text{NO}_2$ = 1 (UP/12 o'clock), front $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ = 2 (DOWN/6 o'clock), rear $-\text{NO}_2$ = 3 (LEFT/9 o'clock), and rear $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ = 4 (RIGHT/3 o'clock). Tracing $1 \to 2 \to 3$ (12 $\to$ 6 $\to$ 9 o'clock) goes clockwise, which corresponds to $(R_a)$ (equivalently $(M)$, since front senior 12 o'clock to rear senior 9 o'clock is $-90^\circ$ counter-clockwise).

questions.questionTextEn: Sequential treatment of $\text{W}(\text{CO})_6$ with (i) $\text{PhLi}$ in $\text{Et}_2\text{O}$ followed by (ii) $[\text{Me}_3\text{O}]^+\text{BF}_4^-$ (Meerwein's salt) affords the neutral organometallic complex
questions.explanationEn: This is the classical Fischer carbene synthesis: nucleophilic attack of $\text{PhLi}$ on a coordinated $\text{CO}$ carbon of $\text{W}(\text{CO})_6$ generates the anionic acyl intermediate $\text{Li}[(\text{CO})_5\text{W}-\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{Ph}]$. Subsequent $O$-alkylation with the hard electrophile $[\text{Me}_3\text{O}]^+\text{BF}_4^-$ yields the neutral heteroatom-stabilized Fischer carbene $[(\text{CO})_5\text{W}=\text{C}(\text{OMe})\text{Ph}]$.

questions.questionTextEn: In the Orgel diagram for $D$-term metal ions ($d^1, d^4, d^6, d^9$), which pair of complexes shares the EXACT SAME ordering of the crystal field states ($E$ lower in energy than $T_2$)?
questions.explanationEn: By the hole formalism and $O_h/T_d$ inversion rule, $E$ lies below $T_2$ on the left side of the $D$-term Orgel diagram for $d^4 (O_h)$, $d^9 (O_h)$, $d^1 (T_d)$, and $d^6 (T_d)$. Thus octahedral high-spin $d^4$ ($[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, $^5E_g$ ground state) and tetrahedral $d^6$ ($[\text{FeCl}_4]^{2-}$, $^5E$ ground state) both have $E$ below $T_2$.

questions.questionTextEn: In double-chain silicates (amphiboles such as tremolite), two parallel single chains of $\text{SiO}_4$ tetrahedra are cross-linked through alternating shared oxygens. The repeating anionic silicate unit in a double-chain silicate is
questions.explanationEn: In a double-chain silicate (amphibole), half of the $\text{SiO}_4$ tetrahedra share $2$ oxygen corners (giving $\text{SiO}_3^{2-}$) and the other half share $3$ oxygen corners (giving $\text{SiO}_{2.5}^-$). Combining $2$ of each type per repeat unit gives $2(\text{SiO}_3^{2-}) + 2(\text{SiO}_{2.5}^-) = [\text{Si}_4\text{O}_{11}^{6-}]_n$ (average $2.5$ shared corners per $\text{Si}$). Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Rearranging the Michaelis-Menten equation into the Eadie-Hofstee linear form gives $v = v_{\max} - K_M \left(\frac{v}{[\text{S}]}\right)$. In a plot of $v$ (ordinate) versus $\frac{v}{[\text{S}]}$ (abscissa), the slope and $x$-intercept are, respectively,
questions.explanationEn: Comparing $v = -K_M\left(\frac{v}{[\text{S}]}\right) + v_{\max}$ with $y = mx + c$, the slope is $m = -K_M$ and the $y$-intercept is $v_{\max}$. Setting $y = v = 0$ gives $0 = v_{\max} - K_M x \implies x = \frac{v_{\max}}{K_M}$ as the $x$-intercept. Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: For a Fermi-Dirac gas at any finite temperature $T > 0\text{ K}$, the average occupation number $\bar{n}(\varepsilon)$ of a quantum state whose energy equals the chemical potential ($\varepsilon = \mu$) is:
questions.explanationEn: The Fermi-Dirac distribution function is $\bar{n}(\varepsilon) = \frac{1}{e^{(\varepsilon - \mu)/(k_B T)} + 1}$. Setting $\varepsilon = \mu$ gives $e^0 = 1$, so $\bar{n}(\mu) = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac{1}{2}$ at any $T > 0\text{ K}$.

questions.questionTextEn: For a binary liquid mixture whose excess molar Gibbs energy is $G_m^E = A x_1 x_2$ (where $A$ is a function of $T$ and $P$ only), the activity coefficient $\gamma_1$ of component 1 is given by:
questions.explanationEn: The excess chemical potential is $\mu_1^E = RT\ln\gamma_1 = \left(\frac{\partial (n G_m^E)}{\partial n_1}\right)_{T,P,n_2}$. Writing $n G_m^E = A \frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}$ and differentiating with respect to $n_1$ at constant $n_2$ gives $\frac{\partial}{\partial n_1}\left(\frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\right) = \frac{n_2(n_1 + n_2) - n_1 n_2}{(n_1 + n_2)^2} = \frac{n_2^2}{(n_1 + n_2)^2} = x_2^2$. Thus $RT\ln\gamma_1 = A x_2^2 \implies \ln\gamma_1 = \frac{A}{RT} x_2^2$.

questions.questionTextEn: In the vibronic absorption spectrum of a diatomic molecule from $v'' = 0$ of the ground electronic state to an excited electronic state, the $(0, 0)$ band is the most intense peak if the equilibrium bond length in the excited state ($r_e'$) compared to the ground state ($r_e''$) satisfies
questions.explanationEn: By the Franck-Condon principle, the intensity of a vibronic band $(v', v'')$ is proportional to the squared vibrational overlap integral $|\langle v' | v'' \rangle|^2$. When $r_e' \approx r_e''$, the vertical transition from the maximum of $\psi_{v''=0}$ (at $r_e''$) directly hits the maximum of $\psi_{v'=0}$ (at $r_e'$), making the $(0, 0)$ transition overwhelmingly the strongest. Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Using the unnormalized trial wavefunction $\phi(r) = e^{-\zeta r}$ for the ground state of the hydrogen atom (in Hartree atomic units, $\hat{H} = -\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2 - \frac{1}{r}$), the variational energy $E(\zeta)$ as a function of the parameter $\zeta$ is
questions.explanationEn: For $\phi(r) = e^{-\zeta r}$, the normalized form is $\sqrt{\frac{\zeta^3}{\pi}}e^{-\zeta r}$. Evaluating the kinetic and potential energy integrals in atomic units gives $\langle T \rangle = \frac{1}{2}\zeta^2$ and $\langle V \rangle = -\zeta$, so $E(\zeta) = \frac{1}{2}\zeta^2 - \zeta$. Minimizing $\frac{dE}{d\zeta} = \zeta - 1 = 0$ recovers the exact ground state $\zeta = 1, E = -\frac{1}{2}\text{ a.u.}$ Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Treatment of $N$-($2$-methylphenyl)acetamide (*o*-methylacetanilide) with $2\text{ equivalents}$ of $n\text{-BuLi}$ or $\text{LDA}$ at elevated temperature ($\sim 200\text{--}250\,^\circ\text{C}$, or $\text{NaNH}_2/\Delta$) to afford $2$-methyl-$1H$-indole is known as the
questions.explanationEn: The **Madelung indole synthesis** involves intramolecular base-catalyzed cyclodehydration of *N*-acyl-*o*-toluidines (such as *o*-methylacetanilide) using strong bases ($n\text{-BuLi}$, $\text{LDA}$, or $\text{NaOEt}$ at high temperature) to generate a benzylic dianion that attacks the amide carbonyl, yielding $2$-substituted indoles ($2$-methyl-$1H$-indole here).

questions.questionTextEn: In an **inverse-electron-demand Diels-Alder** (IEDDA) reaction between an electron-deficient diene (such as 1,2,4,5-tetrazine) and an electron-rich dienophile (such as ethyl vinyl ether or *trans*-cyclooctene), the dominant frontier molecular orbital (FMO) interaction is:
questions.explanationEn: In a normal-electron-demand Diels-Alder reaction, $\text{HOMO}_{\text{diene}}$ interacts with $\text{LUMO}_{\text{dienophile}}$. In an **inverse-electron-demand Diels-Alder** (IEDDA) reaction, electron-withdrawing atoms/groups lower the diene LUMO while electron-donating groups raise the dienophile HOMO, making the $\text{LUMO}_{\text{diene}} - \text{HOMO}_{\text{dienophile}}$ gap smallest and dominant.

questions.questionTextEn: Comparing the solvolysis rates in aqueous ethanol of cyclopropylmethyl chloride (**I**), allyl chloride (**II**), and *n*-propyl chloride (**III**), the correct order of reactivity is:
questions.explanationEn: The cyclopropylmethyl (cyclopropylcarbinyl) cation is exceptionally stabilized—even more so than the allyl cation—by strong hyperconjugative donation from the high-$p$-character bent ('banana') $\text{C}-\text{C}$ $\sigma$-bonds of the cyclopropane ring into the vacant $2p$ orbital of the adjacent carbocation (bisected conformation). Thus, $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ solvolysis follows the order cyclopropylmethyl chloride (**I**) $>$ allyl chloride (**II**) $\gg$ *n*-propyl chloride (**III**).

questions.questionTextEn: According to the nuclear shell model, nuclei with 'magic numbers' of protons or neutrons ($2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126$) exhibit exceptional stability. Which of the following nuclides is 'doubly magic'?
questions.explanationEn: A nuclide is doubly magic when BOTH its proton number $Z$ and neutron number $N = A - Z$ are magic numbers. For $^{208}_{82}\text{Pb}$, $Z = 82$ (magic) and $N = 208 - 82 = 126$ (magic). By contrast, $^{238}_{92}\text{U}$ ($Z=92, N=146$), $^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}$ ($Z=26, N=30$), and $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$ ($Z=6, N=8$, singly magic) are not doubly magic.

questions.questionTextEn: Trivalent $\text{Eu}^{3+}$ and $\text{Tb}^{3+}$ complexes emit intense, sharp red and green luminescence, respectively, when coordinated to aromatic chromophore ligands (such as $\beta$-diketonates) and irradiated with UV light. The role of the aromatic ligand (the 'antenna effect') is to
optionsEn: quench all non-radiative vibrational pathways by forming a covalent $\text{Ln}-\text{C}$ triple bond
directly oxidize $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ to $\text{Ln}^{4+}$ so that $d\text{--}d$ emission occurs
convert the $f\text{--}f$ transition into an allowed $4f \to 6s$ transition
absorb UV light efficiently via allowed $\pi \to \pi^*$ transitions, undergo intersystem crossing to its triplet state, and transfer energy to the emissive $4f^*$ levels of $\text{Ln}^{3+}$
questions.explanationEn: Direct excitation of $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ is inefficient because $f\text{--}f$ absorptions are Laporte-forbidden ($\varepsilon < 10\text{ M}^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$). An organic antenna ligand strongly absorbs UV photons ($\pi \to \pi^*$, $\varepsilon \sim 10^4$), undergoes intersystem crossing ($S_1 \to T_1$), and transfers energy intramolecularly to the resonant excited $4f$ states ($^5D_0$ in $\text{Eu}^{3+}$ giving red emission; $^5D_4$ in $\text{Tb}^{3+}$ giving green emission).

questions.questionTextEn: For an orthorhombic unit cell with lattice parameters $a$, $b$, and $c$ ($a \neq b \neq c$, $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^\circ$), the interplanar spacing $d_{hkl}$ satisfies
questions.explanationEn: Because the three crystallographic axes of an orthorhombic unit cell are mutually orthogonal ($\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^\circ$) with distinct lengths $a, b, c$, the reciprocal lattice vector $\mathbf{G}_{hkl} = \frac{h}{a}\hat{i} + \frac{k}{b}\hat{j} + \frac{l}{c}\hat{k}$ has squared magnitude $\frac{1}{d_{hkl}^2} = \frac{h^2}{a^2} + \frac{k^2}{b^2} + \frac{l^2}{c^2}$. (Option C applies to tetragonal crystals where $a = b$.) Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: According to Eyring transition state theory, $k = \frac{k_B T}{h} (c^\circ)^{1-m} e^{\Delta^\ddagger S^\circ / R} e^{-\Delta^\ddagger H^\circ / RT}$ for an $m$-molecular gas-phase elementary reaction (assuming $\kappa = 1$). The CORRECT statement(s) is(are)
optionsEn: For a unimolecular gas-phase reaction ($m = 1$), $E_a = \Delta^\ddagger H^\circ + RT$.
For a bimolecular gas-phase reaction ($m = 2$), $E_a = \Delta^\ddagger H^\circ + 2RT$.
For a reaction in liquid solution, $E_a = \Delta^\ddagger H^\circ + 2RT$ regardless of molecularity.
A plot of $\ln(k/T)$ versus $1/T$ has slope $-\frac{\Delta^\ddagger H^\circ}{R}$ for a reaction in solution.
questions.explanationEn: In gas-phase TST, $\Delta^\ddagger n_g = 1 - m$, and $E_a = \Delta^\ddagger H^\circ + (1 - \Delta^\ddagger n_g)RT = \Delta^\ddagger H^\circ + mRT$. Thus, for $m = 1$, $E_a = \Delta^\ddagger H^\circ + RT$ (A is true), and for $m = 2$, $E_a = \Delta^\ddagger H^\circ + 2RT$ (B is true). In solution, $\Delta^\ddagger V^\circ$ is negligible so $E_a = \Delta^\ddagger H^\circ + RT$ for any molecularity (C is false), and $\ln(k/T) = \ln(k_B/h) + \frac{\Delta^\ddagger S^\circ}{R} - \frac{\Delta^\ddagger H^\circ}{RT}$ gives slope $-\Delta^\ddagger H^\circ/R$ (D is true). Thus, (A), (B), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about the molecular partition function $q = \sum_i g_i e^{-\varepsilon_i/(k_B T)}$ (with $\varepsilon_0 = 0$) is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: As $T \to 0\text{ K}$, $q$ approaches the degeneracy $g_0$ of the ground state.
As $T \to \infty$, $q$ approaches the total number of quantum states $\sum_i g_i$.
Shifting all energy levels by a constant $+\Delta\varepsilon$ multiplies $q$ by $e^{-\Delta\varepsilon/(k_B T)}$ and leaves the entropy $S$ unchanged.
Shifting all energy levels by a constant $+\Delta\varepsilon$ changes the Boltzmann fractional populations $p_i$.
questions.explanationEn: With $\varepsilon_0 = 0$, all excited terms $e^{-\varepsilon_i/(k_B T)} \to 0$ as $T \to 0$, so $q \to g_0$ (A), and all exponentials $\to 1$ as $T \to \infty$, so $q \to \sum g_i$ (B). Shifting all energies by $+\Delta\varepsilon$ multiplies $q$ by $e^{-\Delta\varepsilon/(k_B T)}$, which shifts $U$ and $A$ by $+N\Delta\varepsilon$ while leaving $p_i$ and $S$ strictly invariant (C true, D false).

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following consequences follow(s) directly from the Third Law of Thermodynamics (Nernst heat theorem) as $T \to 0\text{ K}$?
optionsEn: The entropy change $\Delta S$ of any isothermal reversible process between internal equilibrium states approaches zero as $T \to 0\text{ K}$.
Both $C_p$ and $C_V$ of a solid approach zero as $T \to 0\text{ K}$.
The thermal expansion coefficient $\alpha = \frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$ approaches zero as $T \to 0\text{ K}$.
Absolute zero ($0\text{ K}$) can be reached in a finite number of adiabatic demagnetization steps.
questions.explanationEn: The Nernst heat theorem states $\lim_{T \to 0} \Delta S = 0$ (A). For $S(T) = \int_0^T (C/T')\,dT'$ to remain finite at $0\text{ K}$, both $C_p$ and $C_V$ must vanish as $T \to 0$ (B). From the Maxwell relation $\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -V\alpha$, since $(\partial S/\partial P)_T \to 0$ as $T \to 0$, $\alpha \to 0$ (C). The unattainability principle states that $0\text{ K}$ cannot be reached in a finite number of steps (D is false).

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about $^1\text{H}$ and $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectroscopy are CORRECT?
optionsEn: The gyromagnetic ratio $\gamma$ of $^1\text{H}$ is approximately four times that of $^{13}\text{C}$.
Spin-spin coupling constant $J$ (in Hz) doubles when the spectrometer magnetic field $B_0$ is doubled.
Chemical shift $\delta$ (in ppm) is independent of the external magnetic field strength $B_0$.
Broadband proton decoupling collapses $^{13}\text{C}-^1\text{H}$ multiplets into singlets and enhances $^{13}\text{C}$ signal intensity via the Nuclear Overhauser Effect (NOE).
questions.explanationEn: For $^1\text{H}$, $\gamma \approx 26.75 \times 10^7\text{ rad T}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$, which is $\sim 3.98 \times$ that of $^{13}\text{C}$ ($6.73 \times 10^7$, A). Broadband $^1\text{H}$ decoupling removes $J_{\text{CH}}$ splitting and produces NOE signal enhancement for protonated carbons (D). The $\delta$ scale in ppm is normalized by $\nu_0$ and is field-independent (C). Statement (B) is false because $J$ in Hz is field-independent. Hence, (A), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about homonuclear second-row diatomic molecules ($\text{Li}_2$ through $\text{F}_2$) are CORRECT?
optionsEn: $\text{O}_2$ has a shorter bond length than $\text{O}_2^+$.
In $\text{B}_2$, $\text{C}_2$, and $\text{N}_2$, $2s\text{-}2p$ mixing raises the $\sigma_{2p_z}$ MO above the $\pi_{2p_x}, \pi_{2p_y}$ MOs.
$\text{C}_2$ is diamagnetic with a bond order of $2$ composed of two $\pi$ bonds.
$\text{B}_2$ is paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons in $\pi_{2p}$ orbitals.
questions.explanationEn: Due to small $2s\text{-}2p$ energy separation in $\text{B}_2, \text{C}_2, \text{N}_2$, $s\text{-}p$ mixing pushes $\sigma_{2p_z}$ above $\pi_{2p}$ (B). Thus $\text{B}_2$ has $\pi_{2p}^2$ (two unpaired electrons, paramagnetic, D) and $\text{C}_2$ has $\pi_{2p}^4$ (diamagnetic, BO $= 2$ from two $\pi$ bonds, C). Statement (A) is false because removing an antibonding $\pi^*$ electron from $\text{O}_2$ ($\text{BO}=2$) to form $\text{O}_2^+$ ($\text{BO}=2.5$) strengthens and shortens the bond. Hence, (B), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The correct statement(s) regarding **pyridine $N$-oxide** is(are)
optionsEn: It undergoes electrophilic nitration ($\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) selectively at the C-4 position much more readily than pyridine
It can be readily deoxygenated back to the corresponding pyridine using $\text{PCl}_3$ or $\text{PPh}_3$
The $N$-oxide group acts as both a $\pi$-electron donor ($+M$) and a $\pi$-electron acceptor ($-M$), activating C-2 and C-4 toward both electrophilic and nucleophilic attack
It is prepared by treating pyridine with $\text{LiAlH}_4$ in THF
questions.explanationEn: (A) True: Resonance donation from the negatively charged oxygen ($\text{N}^+-\text{O}^-$) increases electron density at C-2 and C-4; steric hindrance at C-2 directs nitration predominantly to C-4 ($4$-nitropyridine $N$-oxide). (B) True: Oxophilic $\text{P(III)}$ reagents like $\text{PCl}_3$ smoothly deoxygenate pyridine $N$-oxides. (C) True: This push-pull ambident electronic effect activates C-2 and C-4 toward both EAS and $\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$. (D) False: Pyridine $N$-oxide is prepared by oxidation with peracids ($m\text{-CPBA}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{AcOH}$), not $\text{LiAlH}_4$.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following reactions are examples of a **$[2,3]$-sigmatropic rearrangement**?
optionsEn: Base-induced rearrangement of an allyl benzyl ether ($[2,3]$-Wittig rearrangement)
Thermal rearrangement of an allylic sulfoxide to an allylic sulfenate ester (Mislow-Evans rearrangement)
Base-induced rearrangement of an allylic ammonium ylide (Sommelet-Hauser / $[2,3]$-Stevens variant)
Thermal rearrangement of an allyl vinyl ether to a $\gamma,\delta$-unsaturated carbonyl compound
questions.explanationEn: (A) The $[2,3]$-Wittig rearrangement of $\alpha$-allyloxy carbanions, (B) the reversible Mislow-Evans rearrangement of allylic sulfoxides to allylic sulfenate esters, and (C) the $[2,3]$-sigmatropic rearrangement of allylic ammonium/sulfonium ylides are all $6$-electron $[2,3]$-sigmatropic rearrangements. (D) Thermal rearrangement of an allyl vinyl ether is a $[3,3]$-sigmatropic Claisen rearrangement. Hence, (A), (B), and (C) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements regarding the Hammett equation and substituent constants are CORRECT?
optionsEn: For the ionization of substituted benzoic acids in water at $25\,^\circ\text{C}$, the reaction constant $\rho$ is defined as $+1.00$
The *meta* substituent constant $\sigma_m(\text{OMe}) = +0.12$ is positive, whereas $\sigma_p(\text{OMe}) = -0.27$ is negative

For the ionization of substituted phenols, $\sigma_p^-$ constants are used for *para* electron-withdrawing groups like $-\text{NO}_2$ and $-\text{CN}$ because of direct resonance delocalization of the phenoxide negative charge
The Hammett equation works accurately for *ortho*-substituted benzoic acids without any modification
questions.explanationEn: (A) True: Ionization of benzoic acids in water at $25\,^\circ\text{C}$ is the standard reference reaction with $\rho = +1.00$. (B) True: At the *meta* position, $-\text{OMe}$ acts primarily by $-I$ inductive withdrawal ($\sigma_m = +0.12$), whereas at the *para* position $+R$ resonance donation dominates ($\sigma_p = -0.27$). (C) True: Direct conjugation between the phenoxide $-\text{O}^-$ lone pair and *para* $-\text{NO}_2$/$-\text{CN}$ requires $\sigma_p^-$ constants. (D) False: *Ortho* substituents introduce steric and intramolecular H-bonding effects that cause large deviations from the standard Hammett equation. Hence, (A), (B), and (C) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The sum of the formal metal-metal bond orders in the four paddlewheel/dinuclear complexes $[\text{Mo}_2\text{{Cl}}_8]^{4-}$, $[\text{Re}_2\text{Cl}_4(\text{PMe}_3)_4]$, $[\text{Ru}_2(\mu\text{-O}_2\text{CCH}_3)_4]^+$, and $[\text{Rh}_2(\mu\text{-O}_2\text{CCH}_3)_4]$ is _______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
(Given: Group numbers $\text{Mo} = 6$, $\text{Re} = 7$, $\text{Ru} = 8$, $\text{Rh} = 9$)
questions.explanationEn: Compute total $d$-electrons and M-M bond orders ($\sigma^2\pi^4\delta^2\delta^{*2}\pi^{*4}\sigma^{*2}$): (1) $[\text{Mo}_2\text{Cl}_8]^{4-}$ ($\text{Mo}_2^{4+}$, $8\,d\text{e}^-$): $\sigma^2\pi^4\delta^2 \implies \text{BO} = 4.0$. (2) $[\text{Re}_2\text{Cl}_4(\text{PMe}_3)_4]$ ($\text{Re}_2^{4+}$, $10\,d\text{e}^-$): $\sigma^2\pi^4\delta^2\delta^{*2} \implies \text{BO} = 3.0$. (3) $[\text{Ru}_2(\text{OAc})_4]^+$ ($\text{Ru}_2^{5+}$, $11\,d\text{e}^-$): $8$ bonding and $3$ antibonding ($\pi^*/\delta^*$) electrons $\implies \text{BO} = \frac{8 - 3}{2} = 2.5$. (4) $[\text{Rh}_2(\text{OAc})_4]$ ($\text{Rh}_2^{4+}$, $14\,d\text{e}^-$): $8$ bonding and $6$ antibonding electrons $\implies \text{BO} = \frac{8 - 6}{2} = 1.0$. Sum $= 4.0 + 3.0 + 2.5 + 1.0 = 10.5$.

questions.questionTextEn: The Landé $g$-factor ($g_J$) for the ground state of the $\text{Nd}^{3+}$ ion (atomic number of $\text{Nd} = 60$, configuration $[\text{Xe}]4f^3$) is _______ (rounded off to three decimal places).

In the powder X-ray diffraction pattern of an FCC metal recorded with $\text{Cu K}_\alpha$ radiation ($\lambda = 0.1542\text{ nm}$), the first-order $(111)$ reflection appears at a diffraction angle $2\theta = 38.2^\circ$. The unit cell edge length $a$ (in $\text{nm}$) is _____ (rounded off to three decimal places).
questions.explanationEn: The Bragg angle is $\theta = \frac{38.2^\circ}{2} = 19.1^\circ$, with $\sin(19.1^\circ) = 0.32722$. From Bragg's law ($n = 1$), $d_{111} = \frac{\lambda}{2\sin\theta} = \frac{0.1542}{2 \times 0.32722} = 0.23562\text{ nm}$. Since $d_{111} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}$ for a cubic cell, $a = \sqrt{3} \times 0.23562 = 0.408\text{ nm}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
For a dilute aqueous solution of a non-ionic surfactant at $300\text{ K}$, the surface tension varies linearly with concentration near $c = 0.010\text{ mol L}^{-1}$ with a slope $\left(\frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial c}\right)_T = -0.4988\text{ N m}^{-1}\text{ L mol}^{-1}$. Using the Gibbs adsorption isotherm, the area occupied per adsorbed surfactant molecule (in $\text{nm}^2$) at the air-water interface is _____ (rounded off to two decimal places).
[Given: $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}$]
questions.explanationEn: By the Gibbs adsorption isotherm, $\Gamma = -\frac{c}{RT}\left(\frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial c}\right)_T = -\frac{0.010 \times (-0.4988)}{8.314 \times 300} = \frac{4.988 \times 10^{-3}}{2494.2} = 2.000 \times 10^{-6}\text{ mol m}^{-2}$. The area per adsorbed molecule is $A = \frac{1}{\Gamma N_A} = \frac{1}{(2.000 \times 10^{-6})(6.022 \times 10^{23})} = 8.303 \times 10^{-19}\text{ m}^2 = 0.83\text{ nm}^2$.

questions.questionTextEn: The EMF of the concentration cell with transference $\text{Pt}|\text{H}_2(1\text{ bar})|\text{HCl}(a_\pm = 0.010)|\text{HCl}(a_\pm = 0.10)|\text{H}_2(1\text{ bar})|\text{Pt}$ at $298\text{ K}$ (in $\text{mV}$, rounded off to one decimal place) is _______. (Given: $t_{\text{Cl}^-} = 0.17$, $\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.0591\text{ V}$)
questions.explanationEn: For an $\text{HCl}$ concentration cell with transference and electrodes reversible to $\text{H}^+$, $E = 2 t_- \frac{2.303RT}{F} \log_{10}\left(\frac{a_{\pm,2}}{a_{\pm,1}}\right)$. Substituting $t_- = 0.17$ and $a_{\pm,2}/a_{\pm,1} = 10$: $E = 2 \times 0.17 \times 0.0591 \times 1 = 0.02009\text{ V} = 20.1\text{ mV}$.

questions.questionTextEn: At $300\text{ K}$, a liquid has molar volume $V_m = 18.0\text{ cm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$, thermal expansion coefficient $\alpha = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ K}^{-1}$, and isothermal compressibility $\kappa_T = 4.5 \times 10^{-10}\text{ Pa}^{-1}$. The difference $C_{p,m} - C_{V,m}$ (in $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, rounded off to two decimal places) is _______.
questions.explanationEn: Using $C_{p,m} - C_{V,m} = \frac{T V_m \alpha^2}{\kappa_T}$ with $V_m = 1.80 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$: $C_{p,m} - C_{V,m} = \frac{300 \times 1.80 \times 10^{-5} \times (2.5 \times 10^{-4})^2}{4.5 \times 10^{-10}} = \frac{3.375 \times 10^{-10}}{4.5 \times 10^{-10}} = 0.75\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.questionTextEn: The Norrish Type II photoreaction of valerophenone ($\text{PhCO(CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_3$) proceeds with a quantum yield $\Phi_0 = 0.40$ in the absence of any quencher. Upon adding $0.020\text{ mol L}^{-1}$ of the triplet quencher piperylene (penta-1,3-diene), the quantum yield drops to $\Phi = 0.080$. Assuming linear Stern-Volmer quenching ($\Phi_0 / \Phi = 1 + K_{\text{SV}}[\text{Q}]$), the Stern-Volmer quenching constant $K_{\text{SV}}$ (in $\text{L mol}^{-1}$) is _____ (in integer).
questions.explanationEn: Applying the Stern-Volmer equation $\frac{\Phi_0}{\Phi} = 1 + K_{\text{SV}}[\text{Q}]$ with $\Phi_0 = 0.40$, $\Phi = 0.080$, and $[\text{Q}] = 0.020\text{ mol L}^{-1}$: $\frac{0.40}{0.080} = 5.0 = 1 + K_{\text{SV}}(0.020) \implies K_{\text{SV}} = \frac{4.0}{0.020} = 200\text{ L mol}^{-1}$.
